title: Offences, fines and points
summary: What the process of handling a traffic offence looks like, how much each offence costs, how points accumulate and when a licence is disqualified — and what happens when you are stopped.

lessons.title: Two tracks: an administrative fine and a court summons
lessons.summary: Most traffic offences end in a fine with no trial — but they follow set stages, and serious offences follow an entirely different track.
lessons.body:
Not every traffic offence is the same. Most — relatively minor [[term:administrative-traffic-violation|administrative traffic violations]] — end in a fixed fine with no trial. Some, the more serious ones, are genuine [[term:traffic-offence|traffic offences]] in the criminal sense, with a summons to court.

# The administrative track
Most of the offences you might encounter — a seatbelt, a phone, parking, a moderate speeding offence — are handled as a [[term:fine-offence|fixed-fine offence]] or an administrative [[term:administrative-traffic-violation|traffic violation]], under the Administrative Traffic Violations Law, 2024. You get a [[term:traffic-ticket|traffic ticket]] — a notice of a decision to impose a fine — and from there, three tracks:

1. **Pay** — within {{fact:enforcement.violation.payment_days}} from the day the notice was served.
2. **File an objection** — within {{fact:enforcement.violation.objection_days}}, if, for example, you claim you were not the one driving at that moment. An authorised official must decide within {{fact:enforcement.violation.objection_decision_days}}.
3. **Appeal** the decision on the objection — within {{fact:enforcement.violation.appeal_days}} to the [[term:traffic-court|traffic court]].

:::remember
Not paying and not responding at all does not cancel the fine. It becomes final, and can be collected through enforcement proceedings.
:::

# The criminal track
Serious offences — drink driving, causing death by negligence, leaving the scene after an injury, driving while disqualified — have no fixed fine. The prosecution files an **indictment** against the driver, and the case is heard in the [[term:traffic-court|traffic court]] or the magistrates' court. There, the sentence, the disqualification (if any) and the points are set by the court's decision — not by a fixed tariff.

:::law
For some of the "severe" administrative violations — such as a large speeding offence or dangerous overtaking — a police officer also has the power to disqualify the licence immediately, for a fixed period, in addition to the fine. Details are in "Licence disqualification" below.
:::

# What the two tracks have in common
In both tracks you can accumulate [[term:demerit-points|points]] (next lesson), and for an offence that caused an accident, the handling is always stricter. The type of track (administrative or criminal) is fixed in advance for each offence by law — not chosen by the officer.

:::tip
Got a ticket you think is wrong? Do not ignore it. File an objection in time — that is the lawful way, and ignoring the penalty only makes things worse.
:::
keyPoints: Most traffic offences are administrative [[term:administrative-traffic-violation|traffic violations]] with a fixed fine; serious offences are a criminal [[term:traffic-offence|traffic offence]] with a court summons.

For an administrative fine: pay within {{fact:enforcement.violation.payment_days}}, or file an objection within {{fact:enforcement.violation.objection_days}}, and then you can appeal within {{fact:enforcement.violation.appeal_days}}.
Ignoring a ticket does not cancel it — it becomes final and can be collected.
Criminal offences are heard in court, which sets the sentence, disqualification and points — not according to a fixed tariff.

lessons.title: Common offences: fines and points
lessons.summary: A table of the offences every driver runs into — how much each one costs, and how many points it adds.
lessons.body:
Every administrative [[term:offence|offence]] is priced in advance in the Traffic Order (Fixed-Fine Offences), with a fixed number of points set alongside it in the Sixth Schedule to the Regulations. Here are some of the offences that most drivers run into.

# Phone, seatbelt and children
| Offence | Fine | Points |
|---|---|---|
| Holding or using a handheld mobile phone without hands-free | {{fine:phone-handheld}} | {{points:phone-handheld}} |
| Driving without a seatbelt fastened (driver) | {{fine:seatbelt-driver}} | {{points:seatbelt-driver}} |
| Carrying an unbelted passenger | {{fine:seatbelt-passenger}} | {{points:seatbelt-passenger}} |
| Carrying a child under 3 without a suitable child seat | {{fine:child-under-3-no-seat}} | {{points:child-under-3-no-seat}} |

# Traffic lights, signs and right of way
| Offence | Fine | Points |
|---|---|---|
| Driving through a red traffic light | {{fine:red-light-main}} | {{points:red-light-main}} |
| Not stopping at a "Stop" sign | {{fine:stop-sign}} | {{points:stop-sign}} |
| Not giving way to a pedestrian on a crossing | {{fine:pedestrian-crossing}} | {{points:pedestrian-crossing}} |
| Crossing a continuous dividing line | {{fine:continuous-line}} | {{points:continuous-line}} |

# Speed
Speeding offences are priced **according to the size of the excess**, not at a flat rate — full details in [[chapter:speed-distance|Speed, distance and braking]]:

| Excess on an urban road | Fine | Points |
|---|---|---|
| Up to 20 km/h | {{fine:speed-urban-20}} | {{points:speed-urban-20}} |
| 21 to 30 km/h | {{fine:speed-urban-21-30}} | {{points:speed-urban-21-30}} |
| 31 to 40 km/h | {{fine:speed-urban-31-40}} | {{points:speed-urban-31-40}} |

:::warn
For an excess of 31 to 40 km/h on an urban road (or 41 to 50 on a non-urban road), a police officer has the discretion to disqualify the licence immediately, for up to {{fact:police.suspension.offence_days}}, in addition to the fine and the points.
:::

# Parking and carelessness
| Offence | Fine | Points |
|---|---|---|
| Blocking a disabled driver's car parked in a disabled parking space | {{fine:parking-disabled-blocking}} | {{points:parking-disabled-blocking}} |
| Driving without sufficient care | {{fine:no-care-general}} | {{points:no-care-general}} |
| Not keeping a sufficient gap between vehicles | {{fine:following-distance}} | {{points:following-distance}} |

:::tip
Note: not every offence that carries a fine also carries points (for example, illegal parking — a fine with no points in most cases), and not every serious offence has a fixed fine — some (like driving without insurance) have no fine amount at all, because they go straight to court.
:::
keyPoints: Every offence is priced in advance — the fine and the points are fixed by law, not at the officer's discretion.
A speeding offence is priced according to the size of the excess, not at a flat rate.
For large speeding excesses, a police officer also has the discretion to disqualify the licence immediately.
Not every offence has both a fine and points — and the most serious offences have no fine tariff at all.

lessons.title: The points register
lessons.summary: Points accumulate automatically from a conviction, build up to a threshold that requires a course, and then disqualification.
lessons.body:
[[term:demerit-points|Points]] are not a punishment in themselves — they are a mechanism that tracks a pattern: a driver who racks up many offences is more dangerous, even if each individual offence is minor.

# How points accumulate
:::law
If a licence holder is convicted of an offence from the Sixth Schedule to the Regulations, or a final decision on a violation is made against them, they are charged with the number of points set alongside that offence (reg. 544).
:::

Committed several offences in one indictment, or in several fine notices served together? Only the points for the **most serious** offence among them are recorded, not the sum of them all (reg. 546).

:::remember
Old information does not count: if the notice of the conviction or the violation reaches the Licensing Authority {{fact:points.registry-lag}} or more after the date of the conviction, the points are not recorded at all (reg. 545(b)).
:::

# How long points stay valid
Currently, points are valid for {{fact:points.validity.until-2027-05-21}} from the date the offence was committed. From 21 May 2027, validity will change according to the severity of the offence — {{fact:points.validity.from-2027-05-21}} for minor offences, and longer for serious ones; and anyone who has accumulated {{fact:points.long_validity.threshold}} or more in under {{fact:points.long_validity.window}} has their points valid for {{fact:points.long_validity.years}} (reg. 547).

# The scale
| Valid points | Result |
|---|---|
| {{fact:points.basic-course}} or more | Compulsory basic "Correct Driving" course with a test at the end |
| {{fact:points.advanced-course}} or more | Compulsory advanced "Correct Driving" course (only after the basic one) |
| {{fact:points.disqualification-3m}} or more | Licence disqualification for {{fact:points.disqualification-3m.period}} |
| {{fact:points.disqualification-9m}} or more, or a repeat disqualification within {{fact:points.repeat_disqualification_window}} | Licence disqualification for {{fact:points.disqualification-9m.period}}, with renewal only after medical checks and re-examination |

:::warn
Anyone who misses more than {{fact:points.course.max_absence}} of the course hours, or fails it three times, is treated as not having completed the corrective measure — and the result is more severe (reg. 551).
:::

# What happens in practice
The Licensing Authority notifies the driver of the required corrective measure, and they must complete it within {{fact:points.remedy_deadline_months}} from the day the notice was served (reg. 551). Anyone facing disqualification ({{fact:points.disqualification-3m}} or more) may apply in writing and present their arguments within {{fact:points.hearing_request_days}} before the disqualification begins.
keyPoints: Points are recorded automatically from a conviction for an offence in the Sixth Schedule — the most serious among several offences in the same case.
Currently points are valid for {{fact:points.validity.until-2027-05-21}}; from 21 May 2027, validity will change according to the severity of the offence.

The scale: {{fact:points.basic-course}}+ basic course, {{fact:points.advanced-course}}+ advanced course, {{fact:points.disqualification-3m}}+ disqualification for {{fact:points.disqualification-3m.period}}, {{fact:points.disqualification-9m}}+ disqualification for {{fact:points.disqualification-9m.period}}.
Information that reaches the Licensing Authority {{fact:points.registry-lag}} or more after the conviction is not recorded.

lessons.title: Licence disqualification
lessons.summary: Court disqualification versus immediate disqualification by a police officer — two entirely different tracks, with a right of appeal in both.
lessons.body:
[[term:disqualification|Disqualification]] takes away a driver's right to hold or obtain a driving licence. It has two completely different sources.

# Court disqualification
A court that has convicted a driver of an offence may disqualify them — for a fixed period or for life — in addition to any other sentence. This happens, for example, in offences that caused a fatal accident, driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs, leaving the scene after an injury, and driving without compulsory insurance (where the minimum disqualification is {{fact:insurance.no_insurance.min_disqualification}}). The court weighs the circumstances of the case, and is not bound by a fixed tariff.

# Immediate disqualification by a police officer — [[term:administrative-license-revocation|administrative licence revocation]]
:::law
If a police officer has reasonable grounds to believe a driver committed, in their presence, an offence from the Fourth Schedule to the Ordinance, or that an offence the driver committed caused an accident with a death, an injury or damage to property, the officer may require the driver to accompany them to a police officer of rank, or **take the driving licence away from them** (Traffic Ordinance, section 47).
:::

If the officer took the licence — the driver receives a confirmation of this (which serves as a temporary licence) and is summoned to appear before a police officer of the rank of inspector or above within {{fact:police.suspension.appear_days}}. The officer decides on disqualification, according to the type of case:

| Case | Disqualification period |
|---|---|
| An accident in which a person was killed | {{fact:police.suspension.fatal_accident_days}} |
| An accident in which a person was injured or property was damaged | up to {{fact:police.suspension.injury_accident_days}} |
| An offence from the Fourth Schedule (with no accident) | up to {{fact:police.suspension.offence_days}} |

:::remember
The disqualification starts from the moment of the decision, not from the moment the licence was taken. If no indictment is filed within {{fact:police.suspension.void_no_indictment_months}} of the disqualification — it is cancelled automatically, unless the court orders otherwise (section 50).
:::

# How to dispute a disqualification
Anyone disqualified by a police officer may ask the court to cancel the disqualification (section 48), and may also apply for a review or an appeal under the Criminal Procedure Law (section 49). This is a right separate from presenting arguments before sentencing — the application is filed **after** the disqualification is already in effect.

# How disqualification differs from an expired licence
An expired licence is an administrative matter — it can be renewed by paying a fee and sometimes a test. Disqualification is an active ban: even holding a valid licence, you may not use it, and driving while disqualified is a serious offence in its own right, tried in court (see [[chapter:licensing|Licensing, documents and new drivers]]).
keyPoints: Court disqualification is set according to the circumstances of the case, with no fixed tariff; for driving without insurance — a minimum of {{fact:insurance.no_insurance.min_disqualification}}.

Immediate disqualification by a police officer (section 47) is possible for an offence from the Fourth Schedule or an accident with a casualty — up to {{fact:police.suspension.fatal_accident_days}} for a fatal accident.
If no indictment is filed within {{fact:police.suspension.void_no_indictment_months}} of a police disqualification — it is cancelled automatically.
Driving while disqualified is a serious offence in its own right, even if the physical licence is still in the driver's hand.

lessons.title: Being stopped by a police officer: what happens and what they may require
lessons.summary: Which documents to show, what happens in a drink-driving test, and why refusing the test counts as if you had driven drunk.
lessons.body:
Been stopped? The safest and most lawful thing to do is to cooperate: slow down, move right, stop in a safe place, and wait for the officer to approach.

# What they may require
A police officer may require you to show your driving licence, and sometimes also the vehicle licence and proof of insurance. Not showing a driving licence when required, or driving without a valid licence of the right class for the vehicle, are offences in their own right (see [[chapter:licensing|Licensing, documents and new drivers]]).

# Drink-driving test
:::law
A police officer may require a driver to give a breath sample, a urine sample or a blood sample, under section 64B of the Traffic Ordinance. Before the test, the officer must explain its purpose, ask for the driver's consent, and make clear to them the legal meaning of refusal.
:::

:::danger
Refusing to give a sample is treated **as if the driver had committed the drink-driving offence itself** (section 64D) — in other words, refusing does not "save" you from the test, it is equivalent to it in legal consequence.
:::

Someone who is not a suspect can be detained for a drink-driving test for {{fact:alcohol.detention_non_suspect}} at most. {{fact:alcohol.presumption_hours}} is the length of time during which the alcohol concentration measured is treated as if it had also been in the driver's body in the hours before the test — in other words, you cannot argue "I only drank after I stopped the car".

# What else a police officer may do
- **Take away the driving licence** and disqualify it immediately in serious offences or an accident with a casualty (see "Licence disqualification").
- **Take away the vehicle licence** or issue a notice prohibiting the vehicle's use, when there is a concern that an indictment will be filed against the driver.
- **Give instructions** that override signs and traffic lights (see [[chapter:road-basics|The road and its users]]).

# The officer's identification
A police officer not in uniform must identify themselves with a warrant card before giving instructions or requiring documents. An officer in uniform does not have to identify themselves separately — the uniform is the identification.

:::tip
Disagree with an officer's decision on the spot? Not there and then. Ask politely for clarification, and if needed, use the formal channels (objection, appeal, an application to court) afterwards. Arguing on the spot only makes things worse.
:::
keyPoints: When stopped: slow down, move right, stop in a safe place, and show documents when required.
A police officer may require a breath, urine or blood sample for a drink-driving test, and must explain in advance the meaning of refusal.
Refusing a drink-driving test is treated as if you had committed the drink-driving offence itself.
A police officer may also take away a driving licence and disqualify it immediately, and take away a vehicle licence, in the appropriate circumstances.
